newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians turn out in force for Orthodox Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Russians turn out in force for Orthodox Christmas.

text.p: Millions of Russians attended Christmas mass on Tuesday, celebrating Orthodox rites that are flourishing, amid poverty and social chaos, after seven decades of Soviet religious repression.

"We should be glad that we are living in a time when our ancient traditions are returning...and many are beginning to realise that one cannot live without the faith," said Patriarch Alexiy II, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church.

He was speaking at afternoon mass at the newly rebuilt Christ the Saviour cathedral, near the Kremlin, which has risen dramatically in just two years on the site of an identical 19th century predecessor blown up on Stalin's orders in 1931.

"The Christ the Saviour Cathedral is a symbol of repentance for all that had been destroyed, but it is also a symbol of the revival of the Orthodox Russia," said Alexiy, standing in front of a golden icon screen which graces the whitewashed interior.
Cranes still tower over the exterior of the massive church, which should be completed this year and is a concrete testament to the resurrection of the faith across the nation.
Some data suggest up to half Russia's 150 million people are active Orthodox believers despite years of official atheism.
"We should not be embarrassed to call Russia an Orthodox country," the patriarch told the congregation, saying most Russians had roots in the Orthodox church.
This new state Orthodoxy, encouraged by Russia's political leaders, has worried some of the religious minorities in Russia, who include Moslems, Jews, Buddhists and Catholics.

President Boris Yeltsin, an ex-communist who has overseen the revival of the thousand year-old state church, normally attends key religious ceremonies but stayed away this time after catching a "heavy cold" on Monday.
In a statement on Monday, Yeltsin praised the church for affirming the "high ideals of spirituality and the achievement of unity and concord among the peoples of the Russian state".

New Year, celebrated last week, remains, as engineered by Soviet leaders, the main winter festival of feasting and gift-giving, but Christmas, decreed a public holiday by Yeltsin in 1992, is gaining popular appeal.
One sign of this was a "summmit" in the Kremlin on Tuesday between Russia's Grandfather Frost, associated under communism with the New Year, and Santa Claus, who flew in from Lapland.
The two bearded characters agreed to set up a "hot-line" for future East-West contacts, hosted a party for hundreds of excited children and pledged to spread the Christmas spirit.

Patriarch Alexiy thanked Russia's leadership for its support, but also appealed to the Kremlin to remember the tens of millions of Russia's poor and to tackle the problem of unpaid wages and pensions.
"We urge the leadership of the country...to recognise the urgent need for resolution of this problem," he said in a Christmas Eve address.
Neglected churches across the country have benefited from the donations of some of Russia's new rich minority.

But there has been criticism of the millions of dollars spent on rebuilding Christ the Saviour, although it is private money, when much of the nation is on the breadline. The white-bearded patriarch decried the growing gap between rich and poor.
"At all times the Church has been and remains on the side of the weak and the unfortunate," he said.
But he also offered the Church's backing to the state, with which it had close ties in both tsarist and Soviet times.

"Let God allow the Orthodox Church, which for centuries has been with our Motherland throughout all joy and hardships, to support our authorities and the people in hardships and trials of the making of the new Russia," he said.
